claims.text: The proposed workflow trains and updates a machine-learned interatomic potential on the fly using sparse ab initio data.
The workflow incorporates enhanced sampling and physical constraints intended to retain vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling during thermodynamic integration.
The method will produce accurate free-energy surfaces for both solid and liquid phases near fusion conditions.
A machine-learned potential can provide near-DFT energetic fidelity while reducing computational cost in a multicomponent alloy.
Periodically recalibrating the potential in the transition region will faithfully capture phase boundaries.
Periodically recalibrating the potential will faithfully capture electron–vibration and related coupling effects.
Enhanced sampling will explore representative configurations of both the solid and liquid phases.
Targeted active-learning updates will drastically reduce the number of costly ab initio molecular-dynamics steps needed for thermodynamic integration.
The method will predict fusion free energies, fusion enthalpies, and fusion entropies within about 5% of explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics results.
The method will cost roughly ten times less than explicit ab initio molecular dynamics or TOR-TILD.
The proposed validity range is approximately 0.8 to 1.2 times the nominal melting temperature.
The proposed method is applicable to high-entropy alloys containing up to five or six principal elements, including Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni-based systems.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD fully capture vibrational, anharmonic, and electron–vibration effects.
Explicit ab initio molecular dynamics and TOR-TILD are extremely computationally intensive, especially for multicomponent high-entropy alloys.
Performance may degrade for extreme compositions or systems dominated by electronic correlations.
Electron–vibration coupling in highly anharmonic regimes and retraining stability during rapid phase transitions are identified sources of uncertainty.
